merges.sentence: Instructors may prohibit AI use in their courses.
merges.why: All grant instructors permission to ban AI in their course.

merges.sentence: Instructors include a generative AI statement in their course syllabus.
merges.why: Same act: put an AI statement in the syllabus.

merges.sentence: Instructors clearly tell students whether and how AI may be used, leaving no ambiguity.
merges.why: All require explicit, unambiguous communication of what AI use is allowed.

merges.sentence: Instructors specify permitted and prohibited AI uses with concrete examples.
merges.why: Both ask for specific allowed/not-allowed uses illustrated with examples.

merges.sentence: Instructors state AI expectations at the assignment level, not only course-wide.
merges.why: All ask for per-assignment AI guidance beyond the syllabus.

merges.sentence: Instructors may adopt or adapt the provided sample AI syllabus statements.
merges.why: All permit using and adapting university sample statements.

merges.sentence: Sample AI syllabus statements span positions from prohibiting to freely permitting AI.
merges.why: Same fact: sample statements cover the full range of stances.

merges.sentence: Instructors tell students which AI-embedded everyday tools, such as Grammarly, are acceptable.
merges.why: Both ask instructors to specify allowed embedded AI tools.

merges.sentence: Instructors define what counts as generative AI for their course.
merges.why: Both ask instructors to define AI and its scope for the course.

merges.sentence: Instructors restrict AI where it would undermine foundational skills, as in introductory courses.
merges.why: All restrict AI to protect foundational learning, especially for beginners.

merges.sentence: Instructors integrate AI into their courses and teaching where appropriate.
merges.why: Same act of incorporating AI into courses.

merges.sentence: Instructors design assignments that build in student AI use.
merges.why: All design coursework requiring or practicing AI use.

merges.sentence: Instructors assign students to critique, evaluate or verify AI output.
merges.why: Same assignment type: students evaluate AI output.

merges.sentence: Instructors allow and encourage students to use AI as a tool.
merges.why: Both permit and encourage student AI use.

merges.sentence: Instructors teach responsible AI use rather than banning or policing it.
merges.why: Both favor teaching responsible use over prohibition and policing.

merges.sentence: Instructors teach and encourage students to use AI ethically and responsibly.
merges.why: Same act of promoting ethical, responsible student AI use.

merges.sentence: Instructors discuss AI's ethical issues, risks and biases with students.
merges.why: Both raise AI ethics and bias with students early in the course.

merges.sentence: Instructors teach students how AI works, including its capabilities and limitations.
merges.why: Both teach students AI capabilities and limits.

merges.sentence: Instructors model responsible, transparent AI use for students.
merges.why: Both ask instructors to model the AI behavior expected of students.

merges.sentence: Instructors disclose to students whether and how they use generative AI.
merges.why: All require instructors to disclose their own AI use to students.

merges.sentence: Instructors tell students when course materials were created with AI.
merges.why: All require disclosure of AI-created course materials.

merges.sentence: Instructors review AI output they produce for accuracy and remain responsible for it.
merges.why: All make instructors verify and own the AI-assisted content they produce.

merges.sentence: Instructors keep human oversight of AI-assisted grading and feedback and remain accountable for grades.
merges.why: All reject AI-only grading and keep the instructor in the loop and responsible.

merges.sentence: Instructors get student permission before putting student work into AI tools.
merges.why: Both require student consent before inputting their work into AI.

merges.sentence: Students may opt out of AI-assisted grading and request human review.
merges.why: Both give students a human-review alternative to AI grading.

merges.sentence: Instructors use only approved or university-licensed AI tools.
merges.why: Same requirement to use approved tools.

merges.sentence: Instructors direct students to university-approved AI tools and how to access them.
merges.why: Both point students to approved AI tools.

merges.sentence: Instructors do not require students to create accounts with non-university AI tools.
merges.why: Same prohibition on requiring external AI accounts.

merges.sentence: Instructors do not require students to pay for AI tools.
merges.why: Both ensure required AI tools are no-cost to students.

merges.sentence: Instructors discuss the AI policy with students in class, beyond the written syllabus.
merges.why: Both ask for spoken discussion of the course AI policy.

merges.sentence: Instructors remind students of the AI policy throughout the semester.
merges.why: Both require repeated reminders beyond course start.

merges.sentence: Instructors explain to students the learning rationale behind their AI rules.
merges.why: All explain why AI is allowed or limited in terms of learning.

merges.sentence: Instructors explain the purpose and value of assignments to students.
merges.why: Same act of explaining assignment purpose.

merges.sentence: Instructors discuss academic integrity with students at the start of the course.
merges.why: All ask instructors to discuss integrity at course start.

merges.sentence: Instructors invite students to ask questions about AI use and the policy.
merges.why: Both open a channel for student questions about AI.

merges.sentence: Instructors co-create course AI guidelines with their students.
merges.why: Both involve students in proposing the course AI policy.

merges.sentence: Instructors have students sign a statement acknowledging course expectations at the start.
merges.why: Both obtain student acknowledgement of expectations at course start.

merges.sentence: Instructors have students affirm an honesty pledge on each assignment or exam.
merges.why: Both attach an integrity affirmation to each assessment.

merges.sentence: Instructors tell students how to cite or acknowledge AI use.
merges.why: Same act of giving citation/disclosure instructions.

merges.sentence: Instructors may require students to submit AI prompts, transcripts, drafts or process reflections.
merges.why: All require documentation of the AI-use process.

merges.sentence: Instructors may gather drafts, revision histories and process records when misuse is suspected.
merges.why: Both collect process evidence in suspected-misuse cases.

merges.sentence: Instructors ask students to explain their work and process when AI misuse is suspected.
merges.why: Same act of having the student explain the work in question.

merges.sentence: Instructors hold a supportive, non-accusatory conversation with the student before escalating suspected misuse.
merges.why: All require an open, supportive talk with the student before formal action.

merges.sentence: Instructors treat first AI misuse as a teachable moment with educative sanctions.
merges.why: Both respond to initial misuse educationally rather than punitively.

merges.sentence: Instructors state the consequences of AI misuse in the course policy.
merges.why: Same act of stating penalties in advance.

merges.sentence: Instructors decide the consequences of AI misuse at their discretion.
merges.why: Both leave the misuse response to the instructor.

merges.sentence: Instructors enforce academic integrity policies against unauthorized AI use.
merges.why: Same act of enforcing integrity policies.

merges.sentence: Suspected AI misuse is handled through the institution's academic integrity process.
merges.why: Both route suspected violations through the formal integrity process.

merges.sentence: Instructors report suspected AI misuse promptly to the academic integrity office.
merges.why: Same act of reporting to the integrity office.

merges.sentence: Instructors consult the conduct or academic integrity office about suspected misuse.
merges.why: Same act of consulting the integrity office.

merges.sentence: AI detection tools are unreliable and do not prove misconduct.
merges.why: Same fact about detector unreliability.

merges.sentence: Instructors do not treat AI detector results as the sole evidence of misconduct.
merges.why: All bar detector results as sole basis, requiring other evidence and judgment.

merges.sentence: Instructors weigh multiple forms of evidence, since no single indicator establishes AI use.
merges.why: Rule and fact express the same holistic-evidence requirement.

merges.sentence: Instructors may use detector results only as preliminary or supporting evidence.
merges.why: Both permit detectors as a supplementary starting point.

merges.sentence: Instructors do not run student work through AI detection tools.
merges.why: Same prohibition on using detectors on student work.

merges.sentence: Instructors may use AI detection or plagiarism tools on student work.
merges.why: Same permission to use detection tools.

merges.sentence: AI detectors are biased against non-native English speakers and other student groups.
merges.why: Same fact about detector bias.

merges.sentence: Instructors tell students in advance whether and how they will use AI detection tools.
merges.why: Both require advance disclosure of detection methods.

merges.sentence: Instructors compare suspicious work with the student's earlier writing to spot style changes.
merges.why: Rule and fact describe the same style-comparison check.

merges.sentence: Instructors check citations, since fabricated sources can signal AI-written work.
merges.why: Rule and fact describe the same fabricated-citation check.

merges.sentence: Instructors base AI misconduct cases on documented evidence, not suspicion alone.
merges.why: All require concrete documented evidence before acting.

merges.sentence: Instructors move exams and major assessments to in-person, supervised formats.
merges.why: All shift assessment to in-person, restricted conditions.

merges.sentence: Instructors may use lockdown browsers or proctoring tools for assessments.
merges.why: Both permit proctoring and lockdown tools.

merges.sentence: Instructors build oral explanation or defense of work into assessments.
merges.why: Both make oral presentation of work part of assessment.

merges.sentence: Instructors run their own assignments through AI tools to see how AI handles them.
merges.why: Same act of testing assignments in AI.

merges.sentence: Instructors break large assignments into smaller staged parts.
merges.why: Same scaffolding of assignments into steps.

merges.sentence: Instructors use frequent low-stakes assessments instead of heavily weighted high-stakes ones.
merges.why: Both reduce high-stakes weighting.

merges.sentence: Instructors may require students to work on platforms that record version history.
merges.why: Both require version-history-capturing platforms.

merges.sentence: Instructors weigh whether AI would support or hinder student learning in each course or task.
merges.why: Both weigh AI's effect on skill development when designing.

merges.sentence: Instructors base AI decisions on their course learning objectives.
merges.why: All ground permitted AI use in learning objectives.

merges.sentence: Instructors revisit and update their course AI policy over time.
merges.why: Same act of periodically revising the policy.

merges.sentence: Instructors align course AI policies with department and program guidelines.
merges.why: Same act of aligning with unit-level policy.

merges.sentence: Instructors align course AI policies with university policies and principles.
merges.why: Both align course policy with institutional rules.

merges.sentence: Instructors discuss AI approaches with colleagues and seek shared practice.
merges.why: Same act of peer discussion about AI.

merges.sentence: Instructors learn what AI can and cannot do before using or teaching with it.
merges.why: All ask instructors to understand AI capabilities and limits.

merges.sentence: Instructors read university and school AI guidelines before teaching.
merges.why: Same act of reviewing institutional AI policy beforehand.

merges.sentence: Instructors draw on the institution's AI teaching guides and resources.
merges.why: Same act of using provided teaching resources.

merges.sentence: Instructors keep learning about AI over time through professional development.
merges.why: Same ongoing-learning expectation.

merges.sentence: Instructors may consult teaching centers or support offices about AI.
merges.why: Same act of seeking expert support.

merges.sentence: Instructors share AI literacy guides and resources with students.
merges.why: All point students to AI resources.

merges.sentence: Instructors remind students of available academic support resources.
merges.why: Same act of connecting students to support.

merges.sentence: AI can support instructors in course design, materials, assessment and grading.
merges.why: Same description of instructor AI uses.

merges.sentence: Instructors use AI to augment, not replace, their teaching, expertise and judgment.
merges.why: All forbid AI replacing the instructor's role.

merges.sentence: Instructors design assignments that AI cannot easily complete for students.
merges.why: Both design work resistant to AI substitution.

merges.sentence: Instructors state whether students may upload course materials to AI tools.
merges.why: Both govern student uploading of course materials.

merges.sentence: Instructors do not design courses around surveillance or policing AI use.
merges.why: Both reject policing as the course design goal.

merges.sentence: AI features are often built into tools without clear labeling, so users may not know.
merges.why: Same fact about unlabeled AI.

merges.sentence: Clear AI expectations help students understand the rules and reduce confusion.
merges.why: Same reason for clear communication.

merges.sentence: Instructors coordinate with disability services on how accommodations fit AI expectations.
merges.why: Both involve accessibility offices in AI accommodations.

merges.sentence: Instructors weigh AI's benefits, risks, ethics and their own values before setting policy.
merges.why: Both ask for reflection on AI before deciding course use.

merges.sentence: Instructors may use provided tools and guides to draft their course AI policy.
merges.why: Same use of support tools to build policy.

merges.sentence: Instructors develop a clear course AI policy.
merges.why: Both require a clear course-level AI policy.
